Labored breathing with bluish lips is a **life-threatening emergency**, often meaning dangerously low oxygen. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112 or your local number); home treatment is not safe. Put the phone on speaker, follow the dispatcher’s instructions, unlock the door, and do not leave them alone or drive them yourself unless emergency services explicitly direct you.

Keep them sitting upright in the position that makes breathing easiest, loosen tight clothing, and avoid food, drink, or unprescribed medication. If they have prescribed rescue oxygen or an inhaler, help them use it exactly as directed. If they become unresponsive and are not breathing normally, start CPR—hard, fast chest compressions in the center of the chest—and use an AED if available.

Please seek urgent medical evaluation tonight. If it was more than a few streaks, is continuing, or you have shortness of breath, chest pain, weakness/dizziness, fever, a rapid heartbeat, or take blood thinners, call emergency services now—do not drive yourself.

For tonight, keep lights low, avoid clock-checking, and if you’re awake for about 20 minutes, get out of bed for a quiet activity until sleepy. Keep the same wake time tomorrow, avoid naps and late caffeine, and reserve bed for sleep. If insomnia lasts more than a few weeks, disrupts daytime functioning, or comes with loud snoring, breathing pauses, restless legs, depression, or unusually high energy with little need for sleep, contact a clinician; CBT-I is the most effective long-term treatment. If you feel unsafe or might harm yourself tonight, contact emergency services or a crisis line immediately (U.S./Canada: call or text 988).

Stomach pain has many causes. Seek emergency care now if it is severe or sudden, your abdomen is rigid/swollen, you have chest pain, fainting, trouble breathing, repeated vomiting, blood or coffee-ground vomit, black/bloody stool, fever with worsening pain, or pain in the right lower abdomen—especially if pregnant or possibly pregnant. Otherwise, rest, sip fluids, eat bland small meals, avoid alcohol and fatty/spicy foods, and avoid ibuprofen/naproxen or aspirin because they can worsen stomach irritation; acetaminophen may be safer if you normally can take it. Arrange medical evaluation if pain lasts more than 24–48 hours, keeps returning, or comes with weight loss, persistent vomiting, urinary symptoms, or fever.
